PAPER: Journal of Business Ethics (2026) 203:217–240 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-025-06067-w ORIGINAL PAPER Consumption Populism: How Business Leaders Use Populist Logic to Shape Consumption Shafiullah Anis1 · Juliana Angeline French1 Received: 5 August 2024 / Accepted: 24 June 2025 / Published online: 10 July 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract The populist turn in politics has inspired extensive scholarship across disciplines; however, the role of populist business lead- ers remains under-theorized. This article addresses this gap by introducing the concept of consumption populism. Drawing on Ernesto Laclau’s conceptualization of populism, we examine the case of Baba Ramdev—a far-right Hindu-nationalist yoga guru turned businessman in India—who promotes neo-Swadeshi consumption populism. Our contribution lies in concep- tualizing a non-essentialist understanding of consumption populism as a process of constructing “the people” without any predefined essence. This is underscored through the application of the discursive-hegemonic model of market constitution. A key contribution of this study is the development of a three-stage process model for consumption populism, illustrating how business leaders articulate and practice it through three interrelated logics: otherization, homogenization, and hegemony. These logics are enacted via three distinct practices: mobilizing affect, creating spectacles, and posing impossible demands. Additionally, we explore the critical role of affect in constructing collective populist identity. The article also examines the ethical implications of exclusionary consumption populism on vulnerable consumers, interrogates the role of neo-liberal business elites in perpetuating these dynamics, and considers the possibilities of a non-exclusionary form of consumption populism where antagonism is replaced with an agonistic logic. JSON: Name: consumption_populism_experiment Title: A mixed-method experimental and discursive-hegemonic study to test whether exposure to business-leader consumption-populist messaging alters consumer preferences and market attitudes Short Hypothesis: Exposure to business-leader-produced consumption-populist messaging (vs. neutral commercial messaging) causes a statistically significant increase in self-reported likelihood to purchase domestic-branded products and a statistically significant decrease in attitudes toward foreign-branded products. Related Work: Prior work establishes that markets and consumer identities are discursively constructed, and that populist political actors mobilize affect, spectacle, and antagonistic framing to form collective identities. Studies of marketplace phenomena have shown brands can perform populist-like rhetoric to craft consumer communities and that traditional practices (e.g., yoga, ayurveda) can be commodified and re-signified. Existing research is predominantly qualitative or single-case: it theorizes processes (chains of equivalence, empty signifiers, affect mobilization) but provides limited causal evidence about the behavioral impact of consumption-populist messaging. Empirical experiments in consumer research have tested nudges, identity priming, and nationalist appeals, yet they rarely isolate populist discursive components (otherization, spectacle, impossible demands) nor focus on business leaders as the source. Limitations in prior work include (1) lack of randomized exposure experiments that manipulate populist communicative features, (2) insufficient measurement scales for consumption-populism effects on behavior, (3) over-reliance on retrospective or observational designs that conflate pre-existing attitudes with messaging effects, and (4) limited cross-context validation. Abstract: This study tests whether and how business-leader consumption-populist communication causally shapes consumer preferences and market attitudes. We combine controlled randomized experiments with corpus-based discursive analysis to (1) operationalize core populist communicative components—otherization, affective mobilization, spectacle, and impossible demands—derived from a discursive-hegemonic framework, (2) generate validated stimuli from business-leader public messaging, and (3) measure immediate and short-term behavioral effects on purchase intentions, brand attitudes, and boycott willingness. The main contribution is an experimentally validated process model linking exposure to consumption-populist messaging with shifts in consumer choice and outgroup devaluation, plus a psychometric scale for consumption-populism influence. Expected outcomes include quantified effect sizes for each discursive component, mediation evidence implicating affect and identity salience, and cross-sample comparisons that assess contextual generalizability. Results will provide causal evidence to inform market-shaping theory and offer empirically grounded measures for future ethical and policy analysis. Experiments: Design: Pre-registered between-subjects randomized controlled experiments plus corpus discursive coding. Stimuli: 1) Corpus build: collect 600 authentic business-leader public messages (tweets, ad images, short videos) from identifiable cases (e.g., Patanjali/Ramdev) and 600 matched neutral commercial messages (same product categories, neutral brand voice). 2) Construct experimental stimuli by editing/authenticating messages into five experimental conditions: A) neutral commercial control; B) pro-local non-populist messaging; C) otherization framing only; D) affective mobilization + otherization; E) full consumption-populist package (otherization + affect + spectacle + impossible demands). Participants: N=1,500 adults (India sample n=900; comparison country sample n=600) recruited via online panels with demographic quotas for age, gender, education; final per-condition target n≈300 for India and n≈120 for comparison country to detect small effects (Cohen's d=0.20) with power 0.80. Procedure: random assignment to one stimulus set (3–5 items); measure pre-exposure baseline brand-nationalism and baseline purchase preferences; present stimuli; immediate post-exposure measures; 7-day follow-up for persistence. Measures: primary outcomes — self-reported likelihood to purchase domestic-branded product (7-point scale), attitude toward foreign-branded product (semantic differential), willingness to boycott (binary and 7-point), implicit association test (IAT) for domestic vs foreign brands (subset n=300). Mediators: affect (PANAS + discrete anger/pride items), collective identity salience (7-point scale), perceived threat. Baselines: neutral commercial control and pro-local non-populist messaging. Analysis: ANOVA/MANOVA for main effects; linear regression with covariates; mediation analysis using structural equation modeling and bootstrapped indirect effects; multi-group models for country comparison; ablation comparisons: C vs D isolates affect; D vs E isolates spectacle/impossible demand components; follow-up retention analyses. Robustness: exclude inattentive responders; sensitivity analyses by prior political orientation and prior exposure to source. Qualitative component: independent coders perform discourse analysis on the entire corpus to validate experimental manipulations and produce frequency counts for specific rhetorical devices used in stimuli. Risk Factors and Limitations: Social desirability and demand effects influencing self-reported purchase intentions; sampling bias from online panels limiting generalizability to offline populations; prior exposure to prominent business leaders or brands confounding treatment effects; legal and ethical risk exposing participants to hate speech or inflammatory content in stimuli; difficulties in perfectly isolating discursive components (otherization, spectacle) without introducing unnatural stimuli artifacts; limited external validity of purchase intentions versus actual market behavior; cultural specificity—effects observed in the Indian context may not generalize cross-nationally; measurement validity risk for newly developed consumption-populism scales; potential small effect sizes requiring larger samples and greater cost; inability to ethically test long-term behavioral harms (e.g., sustained exclusion or economic impacts) within experimental design; computational or logistical constraints for implementing IAT or physiological measures at scale.
